layer noun

also layers, a layer of, coat (a layer), coating, stratum, in layers

classical

Cato Agr. 18.7: prīmum corium facitō … alterum corium (Lewis & Short)
Vitr. 7.3.8: harēnae (Lewis & Short)

corium, coriī n.

noun, second declension

a layer laid down: of mortar, sand, earth

Its first sense is skin, hide or leather; in building it is a layer laid on a surface, as in Cato’s floors and Vitruvius’s plaster, and Pliny uses it of a layer of earth. So it suits a layer that is put down or built up.

Other words

  • crusta, crustae f. — a hard surface layer, a crust; a coating or facing

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Verg. G. 3.360: fluminis, a crust of ice on a river (Lewis & Short); Plin. NH 35.154: parietis, a facing on a wall (Lewis & Short)

    A layer that covers: the crust of bread, a skin of ice, a marble facing. Also a scab (see scab).

  • tabulātum, tabulātī n. — a storey, a floor; of branches or fruit, a layer, tier

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Verg. G. 2.361 (Lewis & Short); Col. 12.39.3 (Lewis & Short): grapes laid in layers

    Properly boarding and a storey of a building or a tower; Vergil and Columella use it of the tiers of a tree’s branches and of fruit laid in rows.

Examples

  • ubi lībrāveris, dē glāreā et calce harēnātō prīmum corium facitō, id pīlīs subigitō, idem alterum corium facitō

    when you have levelled it, make a first layer of gravel and lime mortar, ram it down with pestles, and make a second layer the same wayCato Agr. 18.7

See also bedding layer, scab, floor.
